red.focus: Separate legal responsibility from moral blame.
red.summary: Learn how law assigns responsibility for conduct without assuming every harm proves wrongdoing. Identify the basic questions about duty, conduct, connection and consequence.
checklist: I can separate harm from liability
I can identify a duty, a breach, and a causal connection
I can distinguish civil and criminal responsibility

sections.title: Harm Is Not Yet Liability
sections.body_md: Someone slips on a wet pavement and breaks an arm. The injury is real, but it does not by itself prove that a shop owner owes compensation. Law asks whether an applicable rule imposed a duty, whether anyone breached it, and whether that breach sufficiently connects to the injury. These questions are distinct. A legal system may recognize duties without any resulting loss, and losses without anyone's legal responsibility. The doctrine of liability explains when the law moves from a harmful event to an obligation or penalty.

sections.title: Different Kinds of Responsibility
sections.body_md: Civil liability commonly concerns a remedy between persons, such as compensation or an order to stop an act. Criminal liability concerns a public accusation that an offense occurred and may result in punishment. Both require a legal basis, but they differ in purposes, procedures, and standards of proof. A single event may give rise to both proceedings or neither. Calling behavior immoral is not a substitute for identifying the applicable legal rule. The law can condemn conduct without making every moral wrong actionable.

sections.title: The First Liability Map
sections.body_md: For a first analysis, identify the legally protected interest, the actor's duty, what happened, and the alleged result. Ask what level of fault the rule requires, if any, and whether a valid defense applies. Do not assume that every system uses a single negligence test. Contracts, torts, crimes, administrative penalties, and constitutional claims have different elements. This compact map organizes investigation before a lawyer can conclude that a person is legally responsible. It also reveals facts still missing from the story.

yellow.focus: Compare fault-based, strict and attributed liability.
yellow.summary: Extend the basic liability map to different grounds for responsibility. Study when the law demands intent or carelessness and when it assigns liability because of activity, status or another person's conduct.
checklist: I can distinguish fault and strict liability
I can explain vicarious responsibility without confusing it with personal blame
I can identify a legal system's chosen liability threshold

sections.title: Fault Is One Choice, Not the Whole Law
sections.body_md: A fault-based rule ties liability to a mental state or failure to take required care. Negligence usually asks whether conduct fell below a legally defined standard of care; intentional wrongs use a different inquiry. Strict liability can impose responsibility without proof of fault in specified circumstances, while still requiring all other elements of that rule. Calling liability strict does not mean that a claimant automatically wins. The rule's scope, causal requirements, defenses and statutory limits still matter.

sections.title: Responsibility for Another's Conduct
sections.body_md: Vicarious liability may make an employer responsible for certain wrongs committed by an employee within the relevant relationship and scope of activity. The doctrine is not a declaration that the employer personally intended the harm. Its exact tests vary across systems and over time. Other forms of attributed responsibility include responsibility for agents or legal entities. A sound analysis separates the actor who caused the event from the person or institution to whom the rule assigns legal consequences.

sections.title: Why Choose a Liability Rule?
sections.body_md: Fault standards may encourage reasonable care and avoid making every unfortunate event compensable. Strict rules may simplify proof, allocate the cost of dangerous activities, or place risk on parties better able to prevent or insure against it. Vicarious rules may put enterprise costs on the enterprise benefiting from the activity. Each explanation invites a counterquestion about overdeterrence, fairness and access to compensation. The legal test must come from binding law; the policy helps explain why that test exists.

orange.focus: Analyze attribution, risk and competing causal theories.
orange.summary: Master how different liability systems attribute conduct and losses to individuals or organizations. Distinguish factual causal contribution from the normative question of which consequences a rule should assign.
checklist: I can separate factual causation from legal scope of liability
I can compare responsibility for risk and responsibility for wrongdoing
I can evaluate uncertainty in institutional and collective harms

sections.title: Causal Connection Has Two Layers
sections.body_md: Even if an event would not have occurred without a person's conduct, law may refuse to assign every downstream consequence to that person. Factual causation investigates the historical connection; legal scope asks whether this kind of loss is appropriately attributed under the governing rule. Different systems use foreseeability, remoteness, protected interests, adequate causation, or explicit statutory limits. None can be applied responsibly without knowing the claim. A lawyer should disclose where a supposedly factual conclusion actually depends on a normative judgment.

sections.title: Attributing Group Conduct
sections.body_md: Organizations act through people, yet legal responsibility can attach to an entity, its officers, particular employees, or several actors jointly. Rules about agency, authorization, corporate fault and complicity answer different questions. Collective harm complicates proof: several polluters may contribute to one illness, or several decision makers to one harmful policy. A court may face probabilistic evidence and an uncertain causal chain. It cannot solve that uncertainty merely by announcing that the outcome was serious. The allocation rule and evidentiary rule must both be identified.

sections.title: Risk, Incentives and Fairness
sections.body_md: Enterprise liability may shift accident costs to institutions that can spread risk, while fault rules may express blame and respect individual autonomy. These goals do not always align. Imagine a hospital adopting a reasonable system that nevertheless produces an unforeseeable injury. Compensation, deterrence and desert may support different outcomes. Advanced analysis states which goal a doctrine serves and which costs it imposes. It then distinguishes a criticism of the rule from an argument about how existing law must be applied.

black.focus: Defend a theory of responsibility under institutional constraints.
black.summary: At doctoral depth, connect liability doctrine to corrective justice, distributive justice and legal institutions. Test whether a rule explains who should answer for harm, rather than merely who can afford to pay.
checklist: I can compare corrective and distributive theories without collapsing them
I can identify gaps between normative responsibility and administrable proof
I can defend liability reform under uncertainty

sections.title: Two Rival Accounts of a Wrong
sections.body_md: Corrective justice asks what one wrongdoer owes to the person wronged, often emphasizing the relationship between breach and repair. Distributive justice asks how a society should allocate risks, resources and losses, perhaps through insurance or public compensation. A liability rule can partly serve both, but they answer different questions. If a person cannot prove which polluter injured them, a public compensation scheme may help without identifying a particular wrongdoer. Calling the scheme compensation does not settle its underlying justice theory.

sections.title: Rules Must Be Administered
sections.body_md: A morally attractive rule may fail when evidence is scarce, courts are expensive, or defendants cannot satisfy judgments. Conversely, an easy strict rule may overreach and deter beneficial activity. Evidentiary presumptions, collective proceedings, insurance mandates and administrative funds can change the system's practical effects. A doctoral proposal must ask who bears proof costs, who is absent from the courtroom, how error is distributed, and whether institutions can administer the remedy without creating a second injustice. Ideal theory does not replace implementation.

sections.title: Responsibility Without a Scapegoat
sections.body_md: Suppose an algorithmic service spreads risk across designers, deployers, users and regulators. Naming the most visible person as liable may be easy but normatively weak. Analyze control over risk, ability to foresee or prevent harm, relevant duties, victim protection and the effects of competing allocations. Separate existing law from reform. Good legal reasoning can explain why a client is not presently liable while still identifying a genuine gap in protection. That intellectual honesty is central to excellent representation.
